archetype.name: Pocket Passer (veteran spot starter)
archetype.definition: At this stage Wentz is a big, stationary QB2 who wins by working the middle of the field to Jefferson and Hockenson, and who pays for it with sacks and loose ball placement whenever the pocket gets muddy.

report.headline: Fine as an emergency starter, but the sack problem is real and long-running.
report.take:
Wentz's 2026 is two games and 48 dropbacks. He took over for Kyler Murray in Week 1, logging 83% of snaps, and started Week 2. Murray has started every game since, and the depth chart lists Wentz as QB2. Read this season as an audition tape for the backup job, not the profile of a starter. The tape is mixed. He posted +0.122 EPA per dropback with no interceptions and a 7.7% TD rate. Under the hood, his CPOE is 40th of 43, his bad-throw rate is 20.5%, and he was sacked on 13.3% of dropbacks, dead last.

The production came from two places: the middle of the field and two very good targets. Throws over the middle returned +0.894 EPA on 12 attempts. Throws to the left returned +0.038 on a 38.5% completion rate. Jefferson (+0.931 per target on 14 looks) and Hockenson (+0.902 on 8) carried the passing game, while Addison's 7 targets went backward. Week 1 against Green Bay supplied most of the value: three touchdowns and +5.0 passing EPA on only 133 yards. Week 2 in Chicago was a 9-3 win where the Vikings defense did the work and Wentz managed +0.5 EPA. That defense ranks first in EPA, pass EPA, rush EPA, success rate and sack rate. It is the reason a backup QB with these accuracy numbers went 1-0 and covered twice.

The numbers hide how fragile this is. The zero interceptions are partly luck: he has a turnover-worthy fumble, and his throws are frequently off-target. The touchdown output rests on three deep attempts and seven red-zone throws he completed at 42.9%. The sacks are not a blip, and they aren't the price of improvising. He scrambled twice for 5 yards, and designed runs lost value. His pressure-to-sack rate was 33.6% in 2020, 37.1% in 2022 and 39.6% with Minnesota in 2025. This year it sits at 66.7% on a small sample. When he's pressured he goes down rather than escaping or throwing it away, and that has been his profile for six years.

Going forward he only matters if Murray misses time. The protection he would play behind is weaker now than when he last played. Left tackle Christian Darrisaw is out with a concussion and guard Donovan Jackson is on IR. Hockenson is in concussion protocol, Josh Oliver is on IR and Addison is out. For a quarterback this sack-prone, losing the left tackle and both of his reliable tight-end outlets is a worst-case combination.

strengths.title: Middle-of-field timing to Jefferson
strengths.body: His best work came between the numbers: 75% completions and +0.894 EPA on throws to the middle, with Jefferson turning 14 targets into nearly a point of EPA each. That is a function of the receiver and O'Connell's play design as much as Wentz. It is still a reliable formula he can repeat in any spot start.

strengths.title: Held up on third down
strengths.body: On third down he completed 76.5% with +9.5 CPOE and two touchdowns, facing an average of 7.1 yards to go. Three sacks on 20 third-down plays dented it, and 20 plays is a hint rather than proof. Still, his late, close-game work (+0.38 EPA, 70% success on 10 plays) points the same way: he doesn't panic in leverage spots.

strengths.title: No interceptions so far
strengths.body: Zero picks on 39 attempts ranks first. The cautious approach helps: 12.8% aggressiveness and air yards right at the sticks. Bad ball placement plus a 5-to-9 interception history in most full seasons says some of this is fortune and won't hold over a longer run.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He was pressured on a middling 20% of dropbacks but converted two-thirds of those pressures into sacks, ranking last among 43 qualifiers at 13.3%. The career line shows this is who he is now. His pressure-to-sack rate was 33.6% in 2020, 37.1% in 2022 and 39.6% in 2025. With no scramble value (5 yards on 2 scrambles) offsetting it, this is a straight cost rather than the price of play extension.

concerns.title: Accuracy well below expected
concerns.body: His CPOE is -7.8 (40th of 43), and one in five throws is charted as bad. Short throws are -12.2 CPOE and passes behind the line are -15.9, so the misses are on the easy stuff. His 2025 CPOE was slightly positive, but his bad-throw rate ranked 55th of 63 that year too, so the misses aren't new.

concerns.title: Supporting cast now thinned out
concerns.body: Any future start would come without left tackle Darrisaw, guard Jackson, Addison, Oliver and, for now, Hockenson. Those players accounted for 20 of his targets and most of his left-side protection. For a passer who goes down under pressure, losing the blind-side tackle is the worst injury to absorb.

trend.note: He produced +5.0 passing EPA and three touchdowns against Green Bay, then +0.5 EPA in a 9-3 grind at Chicago. He took three sacks in each game and hasn't thrown a meaningful pass since Murray returned in Week 3.

nextGame.headline: Clipboard duty behind Murray, barring an injury
nextGame.body:
Wentz is listed as QB2, and Murray has started the last three games with no injury listed in the dossier, so expect Wentz to stand on the sideline. If he were pressed into action, Indianapolis is a decent draw on paper. The Colts rank 26th in defensive EPA and 22nd against the pass, and they generate little heat: 20th in sack rate and 23rd in hit rate. That matters most for a quarterback whose problem is converting pressure into sacks. The catch is that the Colts have been stingy against opposing WR1s (third-best EPA allowed), which is exactly where Wentz's offense lives.

On Indianapolis's side, edge rusher Arden Key on IR and linebacker Jaylon Carlies listed out would soften the front further. On Minnesota's side, Darrisaw's and Hockenson's projected returns land on game day, so their status that week decides whether any relief appearance is survivable. Addison and Oliver are out of the picture.

keyMatchups.title: Colts' soft pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Indianapolis ranks 20th in sack rate and 23rd in hit rate, and is missing Arden Key. That gives a sack-prone backup his best possible conditions. It only matters if Wentz actually takes snaps.

keyMatchups.title: Jefferson vs. a stingy WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: The Colts have allowed -0.16 EPA per target to opposing WR1s, third-best in the league. With Addison, Oliver and probably Hockenson out, Jefferson draws the attention, and the open looks would have to come from depth players.

nextGame.watch: Murray's health during the week; Wentz's relevance begins and ends there.

restOfSeason.body: The base case is that Wentz throws few or no meaningful passes the rest of the way. If Murray misses time, expect a game-manager outline. Minnesota already passes 3.4 points below expectation, and an elite defense lets the offense lean on the run and short throws. Volume would be modest, in the 20-30 attempt range, with yardage driven by Jefferson after the catch. The parts that should hold are the middle-of-field connection and the cautious decision-making. The parts that will regress are the 7.7% TD rate built on three deep balls and the zero-interception line. Sacks around three per start are the most predictable piece of his game, especially behind a line missing Darrisaw and Jackson.

confidence.note: 48 dropbacks over two games, and he is currently the backup with no clear path to snaps.
